full_text_en:
Hainan Timber Company v. Titan Shipping Pte Ltd. and Tat Pin (Pte) Ltd. — Dispute over Damages for Bill of Lading Fraud

Plaintiff: Hainan Timber Company

Legal Representative: Liu Lifu, Manager.

Defendant: Titan Shipping Pte Ltd. (Singapore)

Defendant: Tat Pin (Pte) Ltd. (Singapore)

The plaintiff, Hainan Timber Company (hereinafter referred to as Timber Company), filed an action with the Guangzhou Maritime Court against the defendants, Titan Shipping Pte Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Titan) and Tat Pin (Pte) Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Tat Pin), concerning a dispute over damages for bill of lading fraud in maritime cargo transport.

Plaintiff's Allegations: On July 20, 1988, the plaintiff entered into a purchase contract with the defendant Tat Pin in Haikou City, Hainan Province, for the purchase of 9,000 cubic meters of Malaysian puna wood. After signing the contract, the plaintiff, as agreed, applied to the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China for an irrevocable documentary letter of credit (No. 43OH88573) in favor of Tat Pin, for a total amount of USD 1,831,500. However, Titan and Tat Pin conspired to forge shipping documents in an attempt to defraud the plaintiff of the payment, causing economic losses to the plaintiff. The plaintiff requested the court to declare the aforesaid purchase contract and the shipping documents under the letter of credit void, and to revoke the letter of credit; and to order the two defendants to jointly and severally compensate the plaintiff for economic losses of RMB 2,163,467.68.

After receiving copies of the complaint and the notice of responding to the action, neither defendant Titan nor Tat Pin submitted a defense.

At the time of filing the action, the plaintiff applied to the Guangzhou Maritime Court to freeze Letter of Credit No. 430H88573 issued by the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China on September 2, 1988, in favor of Tat Pin. Upon review, the court found that the plaintiff's application for asset preservation complied with legal provisions and ordered it to be granted.

After accepting the case, the Guangzhou Maritime Court twice lawfully summoned the two defendants to appear and respond, but both defendants failed to appear without justifiable cause. The court therefore proceeded with trial by default. Upon trial, the following facts were established:

In the first half of 1988, the plaintiff applied for and completed the relevant procedures for importing 20,000 cubic meters of logs. On July 20, 1988, the plaintiff and Tat Pin signed Purchase Contract No. MUZI 025-88 in Haikou. The contract stipulated that Tat Pin would supply the plaintiff with 9,000 cubic meters (with a 10% increase or decrease allowed) of Malaysian puna wood, at a unit price of USD 185 per cubic meter, delivery at Haikou Xiuying Port (ex quay), for a total contract value of USD 1,665,000. Shipment was to be made in one lot by September 25, 1988, from Sabah Port, Malaysia, to Xiuying Port in Haikou. Payment terms: a sight letter of credit by bank; a full set of three original clean on board ocean bills of lading marked "freight prepaid"; the buyer must open the letter of credit in favor of the seller, Tat Pin, no later than August 10, 1988. After signing the contract, the plaintiff applied to the bank for loans of USD 1,000,000 and RMB 5,000,000, and applied to the Haikou Branch for the issuance of a letter of credit. On September 2, 1988, the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China issued Letter of Credit No. 430H88573 upon the plaintiff's application and notified the Bank of China, Singapore Branch by telex. The letter of credit contained terms consistent with the contract. After receiving the letter of credit, Tat Pin cabled the plaintiff three times, requesting amendments to the arrival date and the validity period of the letter of credit. The arrival date was ultimately extended to November 15, 1988, and the validity period of the letter of credit to November 20, 1988. After signing the purchase contract with Tat Pin, the plaintiff entered into timber sale contracts with three companies — Wenchang County Material Bureau Production Means Service Company, Wenchang County Planning Commission Economic Development Corporation, and Hainan Hualian Economic and Trade Development Company — on September 22, September 29, and October 10, 1988, respectively, agreeing to sell 5,000 cubic meters of puna wood to these three companies.

On November 6, 1988, the defendant Titan issued a full set of three original bills of lading, stating: shipper: Tat Pin; notify party: Timber Company; port of loading: Sabah, Malaysia; port of discharge: Xiuying Port, Haikou, China; cargo: 2,174 pieces of puna wood, totaling 9,890 cubic meters; cargo clean on board and freight prepaid. The bills of lading were stamped by Titan and signed by an agent. On the same day, the shipper Tat Pin issued a documentary draft demanding immediate payment. On November 16, Titan cabled Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency, advising that the vessel was named "PATROCLOS" (hereinafter referred to as the "Patroclos"), and that the estimated time of arrival at the port of discharge was December 4. On November 18, the master of the "Patroclos" cabled Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency, stating that the vessel was expected to arrive in Haikou on December 1. On the same day, the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China notified the plaintiff that Tat Pin had delivered the full set of negotiating documents under Letter of Credit No. 430H88573 to Haikou, requesting acceptance and payment. Upon examining the documents, the plaintiff discovered: (1) In general timber trade, volume is usually calculated to two decimal places, but the volumes of various log species recorded in Titan's bill of lading and invoice were all integers, which was abnormal. (2) The bill of lading and invoice recorded that among the cargo, there were 1,583 logs with diameters between 40 cm and 59 cm, and 1,095 logs with diameters of 60 cm or more. Such large-diameter logs accounted for 90% of the shipment. It was practically impossible to load such a large volume of large-diameter logs in a single vessel. (3) Titan issued a liner bill of lading subject to liner terms, but the telex from the master of the "Patroclos" stated that the bill was issued under a charter party and subject to charter party terms. (4) Titan's telex stated that the vessel would arrive in Haikou on December 4, while the master's telex stated arrival on December 1. Based on these anomalies, the plaintiff suspected fraud and requested the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China to suspend payment. On November 28, Titan again cabled Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency, requesting the consignee to provide sufficient lighters to facilitate the vessel's dispatch, and declaring that discharge costs were to be borne by the consignee. On December 2, the master of the "Patroclos" cabled Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency, stating that the vessel was loaded with 8,043.43 cubic meters of logs (this quantity did not match the cargo quantity confirmed in Titan's bill of lading), requesting procedures for passing through the Qiongzhou Strait, inquiring whether radar could be used, and again advising an estimated arrival time of December 4. On the same day, Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency replied to the master, permitting the "Patroclos" to pass through the Qiongzhou Strait and allowing the use of radar in poor visibility. On December 13, the "Patroclos" still had not arrived in Haikou, and Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency cabled Titan to inquire. On the same day, Titan replied, confirming that the "Patroclos" had cancelled its discharge at Haikou.

According to relevant data from Lloyd's of London, the "Patroclos" departed Kaohsiung Port, Taiwan, on October 11, 1988, and only arrived at Lahad Datu Port, Malaysia, on November 10. Furthermore, according to information provided by Hong Kong Dadehang Co., Ltd. and a friendly party in Sabah, the "Patroclos" arrived at Lahad Datu Port, Malaysia, on November 10, departed the same day, arrived at Lahad Datu (another berth) on November 23, loaded 1,485 pieces of mixed old wood, totaling 5,537.21 cubic meters, arrived in Hong Kong on December 7, and began discharging. The mixed wood was severely cracked, and the top ends of the logs bore a blue "HT" mark (meaning Hainan Timber). On January 12, 1989, Titan also cabled Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency, confirming that it had issued the aforesaid bills of lading and stated that, upon written instructions from Tat Pin, it had directed the "Patroclos" to divert to Hong Kong, where the cargo was discharged on December 10.

On March 1, 1989, at the request of the International Department of Dresdner Bank, Singapore, the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China returned all documents to the Hong Kong Branch of Dresdner Bank.

Upon verification, due to the defendant Tat Pin's failure to deliver the goods as contracted, the plaintiff suffered the following economic losses: (1) liquidated damages paid for the inability to perform the timber sale contracts with three domestic customers, totaling RMB 561,737.06; (2) fees for applying for the letter of credit with the Haikou Branch and other expenses, totaling RMB 11,341.09; (3) cargo insurance premiums of USD 2,012.61; (4) bank loan interest of RMB 130,140; (5) foreign currency loan interest of USD 45,625; (6) business losses of RMB 649,750.

The above facts are all confirmed by evidence on record.

The Guangzhou Maritime Court held that the plaintiff held a valid import timber license and its import of timber was lawful. The plaintiff's acts of signing the purchase contract with Tat Pin, applying for bank loans, applying for a letter of credit with the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China pursuant to the contract, and signing sale contracts with three other customers were all legitimate business activities and should be protected by law. After signing the purchase contract with the plaintiff, Tat Pin failed to deliver the puna logs as contracted. Instead, without any delivery of goods, Tat Pin colluded with Titan to obtain clean on board bills of lading and, relying on those bills and other forged documents, attempted to collect payment. These actions sufficiently demonstrated Tat Pin's premeditated fraud. Defendant Titan, knowing that it had not received the puna wood cargo from Tat Pin, nevertheless issued clean on board bills of lading for puna wood, and subsequently sent several telexes to Haikou Ocean Shipping Agency to cooperate with Tat Pin in creating the false impression that the goods had been loaded and were about to arrive, providing the necessary conditions for Tat Pin to defraud the plaintiff of payment. The above facts demonstrate that the two defendants, by using the contract and the bills of lading as evidence of the transport contract, jointly perpetrated fraud to cheat the plaintiff out of payment, showing no genuine intention to perform the contract. Pursuant to Article 58 of the General Principles of Civil Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 10 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Foreign Economic Contracts, the purchase contract entered into by Tat Pin with the plaintiff for the purpose of fraud, and the false bills of lading and forged invoices and other documents issued by Titan are all void. The defendants are solely liable for the invalidity of the said contract and documents. Pursuant to Article 61 of the General Principles of Civil Law and Article 11 of the Law on Foreign Economic Contracts, the two defendants shall bear liability for damages suffered by the plaintiff due to the invalidity of the contract and documents. Since the fraudulent acts of the two defendants constituted a joint tort, pursuant to Article 130 of the General Principles of Civil Law, they shall bear joint and several liability for the economic losses caused to the plaintiff. The plaintiff's claims for compensation for losses arising from breach of contracts with three customers, bank L/C opening fees, cargo insurance premiums, business losses, and loan interest are well-founded and are supported. The calculation of loan interest should run from the date of borrowing to the date of revocation of the purchase contract. Since the borrowed funds were not actually disbursed, the demand deposit interest for such funds during that period should be deducted. Accordingly, on September 29, 1990, the Guangzhou Maritime Court rendered the following judgment by default:

1. The purchase contract between the plaintiff Hainan Timber Company and the defendant Tat Pin (Pte) Ltd. is void; the bill of lading No. SH-001 issued by the defendant Titan Shipping Pte Ltd. on November 6, 1988, is void; the plaintiff is not liable to pay the amounts under Letter of Credit No. 430H88573 issued by the Haikou Branch of the Bank of China on September 3, 1988, in favor of Tat Pin (Pte) Ltd.

2. The defendants Titan Shipping Pte Ltd. and Tat Pin (Pte) Ltd. shall jointly compensate the plaintiff Hainan Timber Company for economic losses of RMB 1,352,968.15, and foreign currency loan interest and insurance premiums totaling USD 47,637.61. The two defendants shall bear joint and several liability and shall pay the full amount within 20 days from the date this judgment becomes legally effective.

After the Guangzhou Maritime Court rendered its judgment, it attempted to serve the judgment on the two defendants through diplomatic channels but was unable to do so because the defendants could not be located. The court therefore proceeded with service by publication. After six months of service by publication, the two defendants failed to file an appeal within the statutory period, and the first-instance judgment became legally effective.
